analysis.one_liner: Bans hidden junk fees on hotels, event tickets, and internet or phone service, and stops airlines charging extra to seat kids next to parents.
analysis.headline: The Junk Fee Prevention Act never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required businesses selling short-term lodging, event tickets, internet, phone, and TV service to show the full price up front, including every mandatory fee. It would have banned excessive or deceptive fees, banned early-termination fees on internet and phone plans, and required airlines to seat children 13 and under next to an accompanying adult at no extra charge. It was introduced in the House in April 2023 and died in committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy hotel stays, concert and sports tickets, internet, cable, and mobile plans, and plane tickets — anyone who has been quoted one price and charged another, or charged a fee to cancel a service or to sit next to their own child.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers paying hotel, ticket, and service fees

how_it_helps.text: Businesses providing short-term lodging or ticketing must display the total price, including mandatory fees, in every ad and when a price is first shown, and the price cannot change during checkout.

Ticket sellers must disclose refund policies before a sale, disclose when they do not actually hold the ticket being sold, and reveal the total number of tickets available for an event at least 72 hours before public sale.

The bill prohibits excessive or deceptive mandatory fees and gives the Federal Trade Commission rulemaking and enforcement power, with state attorneys general also able to sue for damages and restitution on behalf of residents.

Internet, voice, mobile, and video programming providers could no longer charge excessive or unreasonable early-termination fees, and the FCC would have to consider requiring disclosure of, or banning, other mandatory fees.
Airlines must seat each child age 13 or younger next to an accompanying adult in the same class of service at no additional charge, with a full refund or free rebooking if they cannot.

analysis.who_pays: Ticketing companies, hotels and vacation-rental platforms, internet and mobile providers, and airlines, which would lose fee revenue and face new disclosure and compliance rules; any cost they pass on would show up in the sticker prices they must now display honestly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ticketing, lodging, telecom, and airline companies

drawbacks.text: The ban on excessive fees uses a vague standard — a fee is excessive if it is not 'reasonable and proportional to the cost' of the service — which businesses argued invites litigation and FTC overreach into ordinary pricing.

Ending early-termination fees and mandatory fees could push providers to recover the money elsewhere, such as higher advertised monthly prices; the bill's own remedy is that those prices must now include everything, but consumers could still pay more overall.
The airline family-seating requirement could complicate seat inventory for carriers and, in the worst case, force free rebooking and refunds that airlines said would raise costs for all travelers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — seeing the real price before you buy — is straightforward and hard to argue against, and the enforcement mechanism (FTC plus state attorneys general) is standard consumer-protection design. The weaknesses are a vague 'excessive fee' standard that creates legal uncertainty, and the possibility that some fee revenue reappears in base prices. On balance the costs are compliance friction for large companies, while the gains go to the general public; the bill was not badly designed, it simply never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, split between subcommittees, and neither committee ever acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on April 3, 2023, joined by Rep. Jeff Jackson of North Carolina.
Sixteen House members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day it was introduced.
It was then sent to the Aviation Subcommittee and the Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee, and no committee or subcommittee ever voted on it.
The bill never received a vote on the House floor and expired at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ticketing services, hotels and vacation-rental platforms, internet and mobile providers, and airlines keep charging the fees the bill targeted, because it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fee-charging ticketing, lodging, telecom, and airline firms

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors — Gallego, Jackson, and 16 cosponsors — were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill never advanced past the committee stage under a Republican House majority.

industries.note: The bill forces full-price display, refund disclosure, ticket-holdback transparency, and full refunds on speculative sales — directly cutting into service and processing fee revenue on event tickets.
Resort fees and cleaning fees would have to be folded into the advertised price, ending the practice of quoting a low room rate and adding mandatory fees at checkout.
Early-termination fees would be banned outright and the FCC could ban or force disclosure of other mandatory fees, eliminating a recurring charge many subscribers pay without realizing it.
Carriers could no longer charge for seating a child next to an accompanying adult and would owe free rebooking or full refunds when they fail, giving up seat-selection fee revenue.
